### 7.2.2 The Dialectic of Free Will: From Kantian Autonomy to Digital Vulnerability

From a philosophical standpoint, the concept of mental autonomy is deeply rooted in Immanuel Kant’s notions of moral autonomy and human dignity (Kant, 1785; Jonas, 1979). For Kant, human beings possess intrinsic value precisely because of their capacity to act according to moral laws they rationally prescribe to themselves, free from external coercion or animalistic impulses. Autonomy is the very core of moral agency (Husserl, 1913). However, when this principle confronts the realities of artificial intelligence-driven behavioral engineering in the twenty-first century, the dialectic between freedom and technological determinism reaches an unprecedented boiling point (Buber, 1923; Levinas, 1961).

The traditional argument from classical liberals often asserts that in the absence of a pointed weapon or direct physical threat, individuals retain absolute freedom of choice—the freedom to close an app, turn off a smartphone, or ignore an advertisement (Calo, 2014). Yet, this argument collapses in the face of what technology ethicists term *cognitive asymmetry* (Hildebrandt, 2015; Farahany, 2023). Big tech corporations and their AI systems possess computational resources, historical datasets spanning trillions of data points, and teams of behavioral psychologists who understand the evolutionary vulnerabilities of the human brain far better than individuals understand themselves (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). To claim that a user possesses absolute freedom to resist algorithmic manipulation is akin to placing a young child in a boxing ring against a heavyweight world champion and then blaming the child for losing the fight (Turing, 1950).

Herein lies the necessity of reconstructing our understanding of free will in the digital age (Floridi, 2013). Free will is not merely the absence of physical coercion, but the presence of intact cognitive capacities that are not artificially distorted by third parties for commercial or political gain (Zuboff, 2019). When an AI system employs dark patterns, emotional manipulation rooted in pseudo-empathy, or micro-targeting based on profound psychological vulnerabilities, it transcends the boundaries of legitimate persuasion and enters the realm of cognitive coercion (Farahany, 2023). Legal subjects no longer make sovereign choices; rather, they are executed through pre-designed behavioral scripts (Weizenbaum, 1976). The paramount challenge for contemporary legal philosophy is how to reformulate the doctrine of autonomy so that it can safeguard humanity against invisible forms of mental manipulation—manipulations that leave no physical scars yet systematically shatter a person's inner integrity (Jonas, 1979).
